## Why This Matters

L13's filters scored every one of 2,003 features *alone*, and that was their blind spot: a pair of features
that carry signal only *together* both scored near zero. A **decision tree** fixes exactly that. It asks one
question at a time, and each question is chosen *given* the answers above it -- so it sees features in
combination. Better still, it selects features for free: **the features it spends its questions on are the
selection.** By the end of the lab, a rule small enough to read aloud -- three questions about a message --
classifies spam almost as well as all 2,003 columns, and you will know precisely *which* features earned
their place.

## A Short Detour: Teaching the Machine to Decide

This is the course's first contact with **supervised classification**, and we take just enough of it to
score and select feature sets -- five terms:

- The **label** is the answer column -- `ham` or `spam`, known for every message we learn from. *Supervised*
  means the answers are known for the training data.
- A **classifier** is an algorithm that learns, from labeled examples, a rule mapping a feature vector to a
  predicted label. The two verbs are `fit` (learn from examples) and `predict` (apply the rule to new ones).
- A **train/test split** divides the data -- typically 70% for fitting, 30% held back for testing. The rule
  is graded **only on messages it never saw**, like an exam of questions that were not on the study guide.
  Grading on the training data rewards memorization, which does not transfer.
- **Accuracy** is the fraction of test messages classified correctly.
- A **baseline** is the accuracy of the laziest strategy. Our data is 13.4% spam, so "predict *ham* for
  everything" already scores **86.6%**.

::: {.callout-important title="Accuracy starts at the baseline, not at zero"}
On imbalanced classes, quote the majority-class baseline next to any accuracy. A spam filter scoring 90%
sounds impressive until you know that doing *nothing* scores 86.6%. The interesting quantity is the distance
*above the baseline*, not above zero.
:::

That is the whole detour. Now we can let a model select features -- starting with one you can read.

## Decision Trees: Selection by Questioning

A **decision tree** classifies by asking a sequence of yes/no questions about the features, one per
**node**, until it reaches a **leaf** that names a class. Here is a tree a human might build for six toy
messages:

| message | digit_count | contains "prize" | label |
|---|---|---|---|
| "ok see you at 5" | 1 | no | ham |
| "running late sorry" | 0 | no | ham |
| "FREE prize waiting claim now" | 0 | yes | spam |
| "call 09061701461 to collect" | 11 | no | spam |
| "are you free for lunch" | 0 | no | ham |
| "win cash text WIN to 81010" | 5 | no | spam |

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    A{"digit_count &gt; 4 ?"} -->|yes| B["spam (2 of 2 correct)"]
    A -->|no| C{"contains 'prize' ?"}
    C -->|yes| D["spam (1 of 1 correct)"]
    C -->|no| E["ham (3 of 3 correct)"]
```

**Reading the tree:** the root question alone (`digit_count > 4?`) captures the two number-stuffed spam
messages; one more question (`contains "prize"?`) catches the digit-free spam. Notice the tree did *not*
ask about "free", even though it is spam-flavored -- "are you free for lunch" is ham, so on these six
messages "free" misfires where "prize" does not. The tree found that out by itself.

How? At each node the algorithm tries **every feature and every threshold** and keeps the question whose
answer best separates the classes -- the split that leaves the two resulting groups as *pure* (single-class)
as possible. Then it repeats inside each group until the groups are pure or a **depth** limit stops it.
Depth is the honesty knob: a depth-3 tree asks at most three questions per message, so whatever it learns
must fit in three questions. And that makes the tree a feature selector for free: **the features in its
nodes are the selection.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Deep Dive: how 'purity' is measured (optional)"}
The standard purity score is **entropy**: $H = -\sum_i p_i \log_2 p_i$, summed over the classes. A group
that is all one class has $H = 0$ (perfectly pure); a 50/50 group has $H = 1$ (maximum confusion). A 75/25
split sits between:

$$
H = -\left(0.75 \log_2 0.75 + 0.25 \log_2 0.25\right) = 0.811
$$

At each node the tree picks the split that most *reduces* entropy from parent to children (the "information
gain"). scikit-learn's default uses a close cousin called the Gini impurity -- same intuition, cheaper to
compute.
:::

## Random Forests: Many Trees, One Vote

One tree is readable but jumpy: a slightly different training sample can change an early split and reshuffle
everything below it. A **random forest** embraces that instability -- it grows hundreds of trees, each on a
random resample of the training data and a random subset of features at each split, and classifies by
**majority vote**. Individual trees' quirks cancel; the consensus is usually more accurate than any single
tree.

The forest also yields a second feature ranking: averaging how much each feature's splits purify the data,
across all the trees, gives a **feature importance** score. The forest's importance ranking and L13's
chi-square filter -- two methods with nothing in common internally -- crown the same leaders. When
independent methods agree, believe them. The price is the thing this lesson is about: **you can no longer
read the model.** Two hundred trees voting is not an explanation; the forest buys accuracy by giving up
exactly what made the single tree valuable.

## Does Selecting Cost Accuracy?

Here are the real numbers from the lab, on the held-out 30% of messages:

| Model | Features used | Test accuracy |
|---|---|---|
| Majority-class baseline | 0 | 86.6% |
| Decision tree, depth 3 | top 30 (chi-square) | 97.8% |
| Decision tree, depth 3 | all 2,003 | 98.0% |
| Random forest, 200 trees | all 2,003 | 99.0% |

**Reading the table:** dropping 1,973 of the 2,003 features cost the tree **0.2 percentage points**. Thirty
columns do the work of two thousand -- the signal was that concentrated. And this is the depth-3 tree the
top-30 features buy:

![The lab's depth-3 decision tree drawn as a diagram: the root node splits on digit_count at 4.5; its left branch (fewer digits) asks about the words www and mobile, and its right branch (more digits) refines on digit_count at 9.5 and message length near 180 characters. Leaves are colored by class -- orange for ham, blue for spam.](assets/l14_spam_tree.png)

**Reading the figure:** the root split is `digit_count <= 4.5` -- the feature you *handcrafted* in L11/L12
beat all 2,000 vocabulary columns to the most valuable position in the tree. Messages with five or more
digits are essentially spam territory (refined by length); nearly digit-free messages are ham unless words
like "www" or "mobile" appear. That is a spam filter you can read aloud in one breath -- at 97.8% accuracy.

## Filters vs Trees

Three different methods named which features matter, and they largely agree:

- **L13's chi-square filter** ranked `digit_count`, `length`, then free, txt, claim, www, prize.
- **The tree's nodes** spend their three questions on `digit_count`, `www`, `mobile`, `length`.
- **The forest's importance** ranks `digit_count`, `length`, free, txt, www, claim.

A filter scores features alone; a tree picks them in combination; a forest averages over hundreds of trees.
That three unrelated procedures crown the same handful -- `digit_count` and `length` first every time -- is
strong evidence those features carry the real signal, not an artifact of one method's quirks.

## When to Use Which

- **Filter (chi-square ranking, L13)** -- first move on any wide matrix: cheap, fast, model-free triage from
  thousands of candidates to dozens. Cannot see interactions.
- **Single shallow tree** -- when the deliverable is an *explanation*: a readable rule, a diagram for a
  meeting, a policy a human signs off on. Slightly less accurate, far more accountable.
- **Random forest** -- when accuracy is the priority and a ranked feature list is explanation enough; also
  the standard second opinion on a filter's ranking.

## Common Pitfalls

- **Selecting before splitting.** Rank features on *all* the data and then split for testing, and the test
  set has already leaked its preferences into the selection -- accuracy is quietly inflated. Fit the
  selector on the **training split only** (this is L13's deferred discipline, now live).
- **Importance is not causation.** "digit_count ranks first" means it *separates the classes in this
  collection*, not that digits cause spam. A spammer who spells out "oh-eight-hundred" defeats the feature
  without changing the message.
- **Correlated twins split the credit.** `length` and `digit_count` partly overlap; a forest divides
  importance between them, so a feature ranked low may be a redundancy casualty, not useless.
- **Accuracy hides the error types.** On imbalanced classes, a single accuracy treats deleting your mother's
  text and letting one ad through as equal mistakes. Scores that separate the two error types exist (they
  are called **precision** and **recall** -- the natural next step, not taught here).

## FAQ / Industry Reality

**"Why not just keep all 2,003 features? Storage is cheap."** -- Storage is cheap; *attention* is not. Every
kept feature is a column someone must compute for every future message, a knob that can drift, and a chance
for the model to learn an accidental pattern. The lab's forest rates 1,280 of the 2,003 features below
0.0001 importance -- most of that matrix is dead weight.

**"The forest got 99.0% -- are we done?"** -- Not quite, for two honest reasons. First, accuracy treats
every mistake as equal, but deleting a message from your mother and letting one ad through are *not* equal;
on imbalanced classes you want precision and recall. Second, "done" depends on the deliverable: when the
*explanation is the product* -- a bank declining a loan, a spam policy a regulator audits -- a readable rule
that gives up one point of accuracy is the better engineering decision.

**"Is this machine learning?"** -- Yes -- `fit`, `predict`, train/test: you have just done supervised
learning. This course stops at using classifiers to *extract and validate information* (which features
matter, what the rule says); the craft of modeling itself -- tuning, validation, the algorithm menu --
fills a course of its own.

## Cheat-sheet

| Situation | Move | Call |
|---|---|---|
| Need an honest score for a feature set | train/test split + accuracy vs baseline | `train_test_split(stratify=y)`, `.score` |
| Deliverable is a readable rule | shallow tree, then read it | `DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3)`, `export_text` |
| Accuracy first, a driver list second | random forest + importances | `RandomForestClassifier`, `.feature_importances_` |
| Tempted to select on all the data | don't -- fit the selector on train only | `SelectKBest(...).fit(X_train, y_train)` |
